name: Shakti side test (10 min per side): hippocampal signal
summary: Murphy's laterality test before any one-sided series: 10 min of the hippocampal 'LTP' signal over the left temporal lobe, where he says it is usually unpleasant, then at once 10 min at the mirror site on the right. It checks for what Murphy calls a 'reversed' structure.
setting: Quiet, dim room, eyes closed, relaxed. One coil above each ear: T7 (left) for phase 1 and T8 (right) for phase 2; the other six stay unused. Note how each half feels: pleasant, unpleasant or nothing.
schedule: One signal per test and at most one test every 72 hours (vendor rule).
notes: The vendor: start over the side where the signal is usually UNPLEASANT (hippocampus: left), then switch immediately to the mirror location, 5-10 min each; this file uses 10 min per side (Skip ends a side early). Murphy uses the result to choose sides for one-sided sessions: a response opposite to the usual one points, in his view, to a 'reversed' or 'left-handed' structure, while 'If you get no response at all, you probably do not have one'. Anxiety during a hippocampal session is his sign that it has run too long, so skip or stop then. T7/T8 is the research translation of 'the same location on each side'; if a one-sided series will use other sites, test there instead. The laterality rule comes from user reports and a small Persinger-lab study (Persinger, Richards & Koren 1994: LTP-pattern fields over the right hemisphere were rated more pleasant than over the left). The hippocampal 'LTP' file is proprietary; it is approximated by a point table in the vendor's standard scheme (3-ms points, about 4 s of latency): four theta bursts, each of four biphasic pulses 9 ms apart (after the 4-pulse bursts of Larson & Lynch 1986), one burst every 186 ms (5.4 Hz, the spectral peak the vendor reports for its LTP signal). The vendor reports headache or pressure in about 2% with hippocampal signals; if so, lower the intensity by one third. Independent double-blind tests of God-Helmet-type fields found no field effect (Granqvist 2005; Gendle & McGrath 2012). Not for people with epilepsy, seizure history or a psychiatric condition; stop on distress.
